  Summaries and exceedance probabilities at locations, population-weighted
  summaries over areas, the uncertainty of the parameters, extrapolation,

---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 5.4,
  out.width = "75%",
  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 150
)
options(RiskMap.messages = FALSE)
# Boundaries and population counts are downloaded once by precompute.R, so
# that the article doesn't depend on those services when it is built.
liberia_boundaries <- readRDS("precomputed/liberia-boundaries.rds")
grid_population <- readRDS("precomputed/liberia-population-grid.rds")
ghana_boundaries <- readRDS("precomputed/ghana-boundaries.rds")
```

A geostatistical model gives a predictive distribution for any quantity that
depends on the spatial process, at any location and over any area. `predict()`
draws from that distribution and summarises the draws. This article shows the
targets it can summarise and the choices that shape them.

## A model and a grid

The model is a binomial model of river blindness in 90 Liberian villages, and
the predictions are made on a 5 km grid covering the country.

```{r fit-model, message = FALSE}
library(RiskMap)
library(sf)

data(liberia)
liberia <- st_as_sf(liberia,
                    coords = c("long", "lat"),
                    crs = 4326)
crs <- propose_crs(liberia, messages = FALSE)
liberia <- st_transform(liberia, crs)

set.seed(2026)
fit <- glgpm(npos ~ gp(),
             data = liberia,
             family = "binomial",
             denominator = ntest)
```

```{r download-boundaries, eval = FALSE}
library(geobounds)
border <- st_transform(gb_get_adm0("Liberia"), crs)
counties <- st_transform(gb_get_adm1("Liberia"), crs)
```

```{r load-boundaries, include = FALSE}
border <- liberia_boundaries$border
counties <- liberia_boundaries$counties
```

```{r grid}
grid <- create_grid(border, spacing = 5)
```

## Summaries at locations

`summaries` chooses what is computed from the draws at each location, among
the mean, median, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, the limits and
the width of an interval, and the probability of exceeding each of the
`thresholds`. The response here is prevalence.

```{r predict-locations}
prediction <- predict(fit,
                      newdata = grid,
                      summaries = c("mean", "interval_width", "exceedance"),
                      thresholds = c(0.1, 0.2))
prediction
```

`plot()` maps the first summary, and `plot_prediction()` chooses others.
Several summaries, or several thresholds, are drawn side by side.

```{r plot-mean-width, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.4, out.width = "100%"}
plot_prediction(prediction, summaries = c("mean", "interval_width"))
```

```{r plot-exceedance, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.4, out.width = "100%"}
plot_prediction(prediction,
                summaries = "exceedance",
                thresholds = c(0.1, 0.2))
```

The probability of exceeding a threshold is often the target that decides an
intervention, such as treating every community where prevalence is likely to
be above 20%. Besides the response, the prediction holds the linear predictor
and the spatial process, which `quantity` selects.

```{r plot-spatial}
plot_prediction(prediction, quantity = "spatial")
```

## Summaries over areas, weighted by population

With `boundaries`, `predict()` aggregates the draws at the grid points within
each area, and with `weights` it weights them, here by the number of people in
each grid cell. The population counts come from
[WorldPop](https://www.worldpop.org/) through `get_worldpop()`, are summed
into 5 km cells in the projection of the data, and become a grid with a column
of counts.

```{r population, eval = FALSE}
library(terra)
population <- get_worldpop("LBR", year = 2020, resolution = "1km")
population <- project(population, crs(vect(border)),
                      method = "sum", res = 5000)
names(population) <- "population"
grid_population <- create_grid(border, raster = population)
```

The mean of prevalence over a county, weighted by population, is the
population-weighted prevalence. The weighted sum is the expected number of
people with nodules, if the prevalence among those examined applies to
everyone.

```{r predict-counties}
by_county <- predict(fit,
                     newdata = grid_population,
                     boundaries = counties,
                     aggregate = c("mean", "sum"),
                     weights = "population")
to_table(by_county, sort_by = "mean")
```

```{r plot-counties, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.4, out.width = "100%"}
plot_prediction(by_county, spatial_scale = "both")
```

Grids from `create_grid()` know the area of their cells, so a cell that a
county boundary crosses is shared between the counties in proportion to its
area.

## Joint and marginal draws

The draws at different locations can be joint, keeping the correlation between
them, or marginal, drawn location by location. A summary at one location is the
same either way, but a summary over an area needs joint draws, since its
uncertainty depends on how the locations vary together. `predict()` draws
jointly when it is given `boundaries`, and marginally otherwise, which is
faster for large grids. `joint = TRUE` asks for joint draws without
boundaries, for example to keep them with `keep_samples = TRUE` for a target of
your own.

## The uncertainty of the parameters

Plug-in prediction treats the estimated parameters as known. With
`parameter_uncertainty = TRUE`, `predict()` also draws the parameters from the
approximate distribution of their estimates, and repeats the prediction for
each draw, so the intervals include both sources of uncertainty.

```{r predict-uncertain}
uncertain <- predict(fit,
                     newdata = grid,
                     summaries = c("mean", "interval_width"),
                     parameter_uncertainty = TRUE)
mean(uncertain$predictions$response_interval_width) /
  mean(prediction$predictions$response_interval_width)
```

The ratio of the average widths of the intervals shows how much they widen.
The difference matters most in small or sparse surveys, where the spatial
variance and scale are poorly estimated.

## Where predictions extrapolate

Far from the data, a prediction rests on the model more than on the
observations. `assess_extrapolation()` flags the locations where the data
leave much of the spatial variance unexplained, or where a covariate lies
outside the range of the data.

```{r extrapolation}
extrapolation <- assess_extrapolation(fit, newdata = grid)
extrapolation
plot(extrapolation)
```

## Transformed targets and standardisation

Some targets are functions of the linear predictor rather than the mean of the
response. The `malnutrition` data give the height-for-age z-score (HAZ) of 2,671
children in Ghana, with their age, in years, and sex. A Gaussian model of HAZ
describes the mean z-score at each location. A child is stunted when HAZ is
below $-2$, so the proportion stunted at a location is
$\Phi\{(-2 - \mu)/\sigma\}$, where $\mu$ is the mean z-score there and $\sigma$
the standard deviation of children's z-scores around it, estimated by the
measurement error variance.

```{r fit-ghana}
data(malnutrition)
ghana_crs <- propose_crs(malnutrition, messages = FALSE)
malnutrition <- st_transform(malnutrition, ghana_crs)

set.seed(2026)
fit_haz <- glgpm(HAZ ~ age + sex + gp(),
                 data = malnutrition,
                 family = "gaussian")
sd_child <- sqrt(coef(fit_haz)$sigma2_me)
stunting <- function(link) pnorm((-2 - link) / sd_child)
```

The mean z-score depends on age and sex, so a prediction needs them. With
`standardise`, `predict()` averages the targets over a reference population,
here equal numbers of girls and boys at each year of age from 0 to 4, so that
every location and region is compared on the same population. A `.weight`
column weights the rows of the reference population.

```{r download-ghana, eval = FALSE}
ghana <- st_transform(gb_get_adm0("Ghana"), ghana_crs)
regions <- st_transform(gb_get_adm1("Ghana"), ghana_crs)
```

```{r load-ghana, include = FALSE}
ghana <- ghana_boundaries$ghana
regions <- ghana_boundaries$regions
```

```{r predict-stunting}
reference <- expand.grid(age = 0:4 + 0.5,
                         sex = c("female", "male"))
reference$.weight <- 1

by_region <- predict(fit_haz,
                     newdata = create_grid(ghana, spacing = 10),
                     boundaries = regions,
                     aggregate = "mean",
                     transform = list(stunting = stunting),
                     standardise = reference)
to_table(by_region, quantity = "stunting", sort_by = "mean", digits = 3)
plot_prediction(by_region, quantity = "stunting")
```

## Learn more

Chapter [4](https://www.mbgr.org/04_geostatistical-prediction.html) of the book
*Model-based geostatistics for global public health using R* treats
prediction, with targets at locations and over areas, and Chapter
[5](https://www.mbgr.org/05_case-studies.html) the mapping of stunting in
Ghana.
